notes.text: Given me — This and the following passages may be in some sort understood of the prophet Isaiah, but they are far more evidently and eminently verified in Christ, and indeed seem to be meant directly of him. The tongue - All ability of speaking plainly, and convincingly, and persuasively. Weary - Burdened with the sense of his, deplorable condition. Wakeneth - Me, from time to time, and continually. To hear - He by his Divine power assists me to the practice of all his commands and my duties, with all attention and diligence.
I gave — I patiently yielded up myself to those who smote me.

Justifieth — God will clear up my righteousness, and shew by many and mighty signs and wonders, that I lived and died his faithful servant. Let him come - l am conscious of mine own innocency, and I know that God will give sentence for me.
They — Mine accusers and enemies. The moth - Shall be cut off and consumed by a secret curse.

glossa.text: *The Lord hath given,* etc. ((ID.)) Although these things can be referred to Isaias, yet properly they are referred to Christ, as though he said: I who once wrought such things can now also work the like; my power is not diminished.

*As a garment.* ((ID.)) A garment is consumed by age and by the moth. The Jews too were called to penance for forty-two years after the Passion: at last, being negligent, they were crushed when the Romans came, and devoured by the moth of an evil conscience.

notes.text: Grief — With continual weeping.
Iniquity — For the punishment of mine iniquity. Consumed - The juice and marrow of them bring almost dried up with grief.
A fear — They were afraid to give me any countenance or assistance. Fled - To prevent their own danger and ruin.
A broken vessel — Which is irreparable, and useless, and therefore despised by all.
Fear — Just cause of fear.
My times — All the affairs and events of my life, are wholly in thy power.

glossa.text: *In a spacious place.* ((CASS.)) The spacious place of going freely to the fatherland of the virtues is charity: but because the flesh is weak and evils press: *Have mercy on me, O Lord.* Now the dread is recounted, that is, how many and how great are the things that disturb, against which is the prayer, *I am troubled.* ((AUG.)) Since he said before: *Thou hast set my feet in a spacious place,* etc. But for some the place is spacious, out of the thanksgiving of deliverance; for others, out of tribulation, it is a narrow strait. *Troubled.* He is angry for the sins of the chaff, etc., *as far as* for the life of the perfect is the advancement of others. *In anger the eye.* In the anger of the persecutors, etc., *as far as* that God may be sought from every degree. ((CASS.)) Or the understanding is disturbed and the mind confounded, etc., *as far as* neither in mind nor in body can there be any presumption of man. ((AUG.)) Anger through vice blinds the eye of the mind; anger through zeal troubles it: because this too, the mind being shaken, scatters contemplation, which is not except with an unquiet mind; but thereafter, after a little, it profits the more toward seeing.
*In poverty.* ((ID.)) Or *in want.* I lack health of body, and the torments are not spared. I lack release, and death is spared; and in this my confidence has been weakened.

*Above all my enemies.* ((ID.)) They live worse than the pagans and the Jews, etc., *as far as* for whom even their acquaintance are afraid, lest all be such. ((CASS.)) Or, among all my enemies, or, held in greater reproach than those who are worthy of it; and *to my neighbours,* to kinsfolk, or to those about to believe; and *to my acquaintance,* to those of the household.

*They that saw me without.* ((HIER.)) *Without,* Christ, that is, those who thought him a mere man. *I am forgotten as one dead from the heart.* ((CASS.)) Or, I have fallen out of their heart, like a dead man whose memory is buried with his body, of whose restoration there is despair. *A vessel that is destroyed,* Jesus dead is thought fit to be cast away.

*The blame of many.* ((AUG.)) They are blamed, etc., *as far as* not any man. *Round about. In that while they assembled together.* ((CASS.)) Of errors, etc., *as far as* that is, by the appetite of temporal things.

*My lots.* ((ID.)) Or, the times of life. ((AUG.)) Because we live or die when thou wilt: therefore *deliver.* Although the order of election is with thee, just and hidden, yet I, etc., *as far as* which, without merits, chooses whom it will.

*Illumine.* ((CASS.)) Make thy good will manifest upon me, that as they despair of the dying, so they may have confidence in the rising. ((AUG.)) *Illumine.* Let it appear who belongs to thee, since now there is confusion; whence elsewhere: *Distinguish my cause ((Psal. XLI))*; yet lest he seem to justify himself, he adds: *Save me in mercy,* not in my own justice.

notes.text: Who being in the essential form — The incommunicable nature. Of God - From eternity, as he was afterward in the form of man; real God, as real man. Counted it no act of robbery - That is the precise meaning of the words, - no invasion of another's prerogative, but his own strict and unquestionable right. To be equal with God - the word here translated equal, occurs in the adjective form five or six times in the New Testament, Matt. xx, 12; Luke vi, 34; John v, 18; Acts xi, 17; Rev. xxi, 16. In all which places it expresses not a bare resemblance, but a real and proper equalitg. It here implies both the fulness and the supreme height of the Godhead; to which are opposed, he emptied and he humbled himself.

Yet — He was so far from tenaciously insisting upon, that he willingly relinquished, his claim. He was content to forego the glories of the Creator, and to appear in the form of a creature; nay, to be made in the likeness of the fallen creatures; and not only to share the disgrace, but to suffer the punishment, due to the meanest and vilest among them all. He emptied himself - Of that divine fulness, which he received again at his exaltation. Though he remained full, John i, 14, yet he appeared as if he had been empty; for he veiled his fulness from the sight of men and angels. Yea, he not only veiled, but, in some sense, renounced, the glory which he had before the world began. Taking - And by that very act emptying himself. The form of a servant - The form, the likeness, the fashion, though not exactly the same, are yet nearly related to each other. The form expresses something absolute; the likeness refers to other things of the same kind; the fashion respects what appears to sight and sense. Being made in the likeness of men - A real man, like other men. Hereby he took the form of a servant.

And being found in fashion as a man — A common man, without any peculiar excellence or comeliness. He humbled himself - To a still greater depth. Becoming obedient - To God, though equal with him. Even unto death - The greatest instance both of humiliation and obedience. Yea, the death of the cross - Inflicted on few but servants or slaves.

Wherefore — Because of his voluntary humiliation and obedience. He humbled himself; but God hath exalted him - So recompensing his humiliation. And hath given him - So recompensing his emptying himself. A name which is above every name - Dignity and majesty superior to every creature.

That every knee — That divine honour might be paid in every possible manner by every creature. Might bow - Either with love or trembling. Of those in heaven, earth, under the earth - That is, through the whole universe.
And every tongue — Even of his enemies. Confess that Jesus Christ is Lord - Jehovah; not now "in the form of a servant," but enthroned in the glory of God the Father.

glossa.text: *For let this be your mind,* etc. As if to say: Let each one not seek his own advantage, but that of others, as Christ did. To patience and to humility I invite you. For you ought to be minded in yourselves in that which was in Christ. As Christ sought not his own things, but ours, so let us bear one another's burdens.

*Who being in the form.* He sets high things concerning Christ before all else, that those in whom there is place for abasement may not disdain to be humbled. *He thought it not robbery.* By usurping what would not be his own, as did the devil and the first man. Or, he did not judge himself to be equal to God according to his humanity, which would have been to commit robbery, that is, to presume upon what is not his own. *But he emptied himself.* The height having been shown, he adds concerning the humility.

((Aug., Ench. c. 35 et 36)). But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, etc., *as far as* it came about that the man Christ could have no sin.

*The form of a servant.* Not losing the form of God: the form of a servant came to him, the form of God did not depart: *He emptied himself.* To empty oneself is to show oneself visible out of the greatness of his own invisibility.
*Made.* According to the form of a servant, he who was unmade according to the form of God, and also by his own *Habit.* That is, by his manner of life.
*He humbled himself,* etc. ((CHRYS.)) Of his own accord the Son obeyed the Father, not as though into a servile, etc., *as far as* that he honoured the Father most of all.
*For which cause.* The humility of Christ having been shown, which appeared chiefly in the passion; now he shows concerning his [Christ's] glory, and what and how much humility merits.

*That in the name.* Here he opens to whom the name of God has been given, to whom every creature bends the knee, that is, to God. But perhaps it might be said that the man was God by adoption, and thus Christ in part true God, in that in part he will be adoptive. But the creature does not bend the knee to an adoptive God, but to a true one. Yet it is agreed that Christ is true God, to whom the knee is bent, not adoptive.

*That the Lord,* etc. Which here certain men deny, saying: How can it come to pass that a man should be in the glory of God the Father? but if he be adoptive, a man who is God cannot be in the glory of God the Father.

notes.text: Mark xiv, 10; Luke xxii, 3.
They bargained with him for thirty pieces of silver — (About three pounds fifteen shillings sterling; or sixteen dollars sixty- seven cents) the price of a slave, Exod. xxi, 32.
On the first day of unleavened bread — Being Thursday, the fourteenth day of the first month, Exod. xii, 6, 15. Mark xiv, 12 Luke xxii, 7
The Master saith, My time is at hand — That is, the time of my suffering.
Mark xiv, 17; Luke xxii, 14.
He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish — Which it seems Judas was doing at that very time. This dish was a vessel full of vinegar, wherein they dipped their bitter herbs.

The Son of man goeth through sufferings to glory, as it is written of him — Yet this is no excuse for him that betrayeth him: miserable will that man be: it had been good for that man if he had not been born - May not the same be said of every man that finally perishes? But who can reconcile this, if it were true of Judas alone, with the doctrine of universal salvation?
Thou hast said — That is, it is as thou hast said.

Jesus took the bread — the bread or cake, which the master of the family used to divide among them, after they had eaten the passover. The custom our Lord now transferred to a nobler use. This bread is, that is, signifies or represents my body, according to the style of the sacred writers. Thus Gen. xl, 12, The three branches are three days. Thus Gal. iv, 24, St. Paul speaking of Sarah and Hagar, says, These are the two covenants. Thus in the grand type of our Lord, Exod. xii, 11, God says of the paschal lamb, This is the Lord's passover. Now Christ substituting the holy communion for the passover, follows the style of the Old Testament, and uses the same expressions the Jews were wont to use in celebrating the passover.
And he took the cup — Called by the Jews the cup of thanksgiving; which the master of the family used likewise to give to each after supper.
This is the sign of my blood, whereby the new testament or covenant is confirmed. Which is shed for many — As many as spring from Adam.

I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, till I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom — That is, I shall taste no more wine, till I drink wine of quite another kind in the glorious kingdom of my Father. And of this you shall also partake with me.

And when they had sung the hymn — Which was constantly sung at the close of the passover. It consisteth of six psalms, from the 113th to the 118th. The Mount of Olives - Was over against the temple, about two miles from Jerusalem. Mark xiv, 26; Luke xxii, 39; John xviii, 1.
All ye will be offended at me — Something will happen to me, which will occasion your falling into sin by forsaking me. Zech. xiii, 7.
But notwithstanding this, after I am risen I will go before you (as a shepherd before his sheep) into Galilee. Though you forsake me, I will not for this forsake you.
Before cock crowing thou wilt deny me thrice — That is, before three in the morning, the usual time of cock crowing: although one cock was heard to crow once, after Peter's first denial of his Lord.
In like manner also said all the disciples — But such was the tenderness of our Lord, that he would not aggravate their sin by making any reply.

Then cometh Jesus to a place called Gethsemane — That is, the valley of fatness. The garden probably had its name from its soil and situation, laying in some little valley between two of those many hills, the range of which constitutes the Mount of Olives. Mark xiv, 32; Luke xxii, 40.

And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee — To be witnesses of all; he began to be sorrowful and in deep anguish - Probably from feeling the arrows of the Almighty stick fast in his soul, while God laid on him the iniquities of us all. Who can tell what painful and dreadful sensations were then impressed on him by the immediate hand of God? The former word in the original properly signifies, to be penetrated with the most exquisite sorrow; the latter to be quite depressed, and almost overwhelmed with the load.

And going a little farther — About a stone's cast, Luke xxii, 41 - So that the apostles could both see and hear him still. If it be possible, let this cup pass from me - And it did pass from him quickly. When he cried unto God with strong cries and tears, he was heard in that which he feared. God did take away the terror and severity of that inward conflict.
The spirit — Your spirit: ye yourselves. The flesh - Your nature. How gentle a rebuke was this, and how kind an apology! especially at a time when our Lord's own mind was so weighed down with sorrow.
Sleep on now, if you can, and take your rest — For any farther service you can be of to me.
Mark xiv, 43; Luke xxii, 47; John xviii, 2.

The heroic behaviour of the blessed Jesus, in the whole period of his sufferings, will be observed by every attentive eye, and felt by every pious heart: although the sacred historians, according to their usual but wonderful simplicity, make no encomiums upon it. With what composure does he go forth to meet the traitor! With what calmness receive that malignant kiss! With what dignity does he deliver himself into the hands of his enemies! Yet plainly showing his superiority over them, and even then leading as it were captivity captive!

And one of them striking the servant of the high priest — Probably the person that seized Jesus first; Cut off his ear - Aiming, it seems, to cleave his head, but that by a secret providence interposing, he declined the blow. Mark xiv, 47; Luke xxii, 49; John xviii, 10.
All they that take the sword — Without God's giving it them: without sufficient authority.
He will presently give me more than twelve legions of angels — The least of whom, it is probable, could overturn the earth and destroy all the inhabitants of it.
Mark xiv, 48; Luke xxii, 52
They led him away to Caiaphas — From the house of Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, to whom they had carried him first. Mark xiv, 53; Luke xxii, 54; John xviii, 12.

But Peter followed him afar off — Variously agitated by conflicting passions; love constrained him to follow his Master; fear made him follow afar off. And going in, sat with the servants - Unfit companions as the event showed.

Yet found they none — On whose evidence they could condemn him to die. At last came two false witnesses - Such they were, although part of what they said was true; because our Lord did not speak some of those words at all; nor any of them in this sense.

Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man — He speaks in the third person, modestly, and yet plainly; Sitting on the right hand of power - That is, the right hand of God: And coming upon the clouds of heaven - As he is represented by Daniel, Dan. vii, 13, 14. Our Lord looked very unlike that person now! But nothing could be more awful, more majestic and becoming, than such an admonition in such circumstances!

Then the high priest rent his clothes — Though the high priest was forbidden to rend his clothes (that is, his upper garment) in some cases where others were allowed to do it, Lev. xxi, 10; yet in case of blasphemy or any public calamity, it was thought allowable. Caiaphas hereby expressed, in the most artful manner, his horror at hearing such grievous blasphemy.

Then — After he had declared he was the Son of God, the sanhedrim doubtless ordered him to be carried out, while they were consulting what to do. And then it was that the soldiers who kept him began these insults upon him.
He denied with an oath — To which possibly he was not unaccustomed, before our Lord called him.

Surely thou art also one of them, for thy speech discovereth thee — Malchus might have brought a stronger proof than this. But such is the overruling providence of God, that the world, in the height of their zeal, commonly catch hold of the very weakest of all arguments against the children of God.
Then began he to curse and to swear — Having now quite lost the reins, the government of himself.

In the morning — As the sanhedrim used to meet in one of the courts of the temple, which was never opened in the night, they were forced to stay till the morning before they could proceed regularly, in the resolution they had taken to put him to death. Mark xv, 1; Luke xxii, 66; xxiii, 1; John xviii, 28.
Having bound him — They had bound him when he was first apprehended. But they did it now afresh, to secure him from any danger of an escape, as he passed through the streets of Jerusalem.
Then Judas seeing that he was condemned — Which probably he thought Christ would have prevented by a miracle.

They said, what is that to us? — How easily could they digest innocent blood! And yet they had a conscience! It is not lawful (say they) to put it into the treasury - But very lawful to slay the innocent!
In that part of the temple where the sanhedrim met.

They bought with them the potter's field — Well known, it seems, by that name. This was a small price for a field so near Jerusalem. But the earth had probably been digged for potters' vessels, so that it was now neither fit for tillage nor pasture, and consequently of small value. Foreigners - Heathens especially, of whom there were then great numbers in Jerusalem.

Then was fulfilled — What was figuratively represented of old, was now really accomplished. What was spoken by the prophet - The word Jeremy, which was added to the text in latter copies, and thence received into many translations, is evidently a mistake: for he who spoke what St. Matthew here cites (or rather paraphrases) was not Jeremy, but Zechariah. Zech. xi, 12.
As the Lord commanded me — To write, to record.
Art thou the king of the Jews? — Jesus before Caiaphas avows himself to be the Christ, before Pilate to be a king; clearly showing thereby, that his answering no more, was not owing to any fear.
At every feast — Every year, at the feast of the passover. Mark xv, 6; Luke xxiii, 17; John xviii, 39.
He knew that for envy they had delivered him — As well as from malice and revenge; they envied him, because the people magnified him.

They all say, Let him be crucified — The punishment which Barabbas had deserved: and this probably made them think of it. But in their malice they forgot with how dangerous a precedent they furnished the Roman governor. And indeed within the compass of a few years it turned dreadfully upon themselves.
Then Pilate took water and washed his hands — This was a custom frequently used among the heathens as well as among the Jews, in token of innocency.

His blood be on us and on our children — As this imprecation was dread. fully answered in the ruin so quickly brought on the Jewish nation, and the calamities which have ever since pursued that wretched people, so it was peculiarly fulfilled by Titus the Roman general, on the Jews whom he took during the siege of Jerusalem. So many, after having been scourged in a terrible manner, were crucified all round the city, that in a while there was not room near the wall for the crosses to stand by each other. Probably this befell some of those who now joined in this cry, as it certainly did many of their children: the very finger of God thus pointing out their crime in crucifying his Son.

He delivered him to be crucified — The person crucified was nailed to the cross as it lay on the ground, through each hand extended to the utmost stretch, and through both the feet together. Then the cross was raised up, and the foot of it thrust with a violent shock into a hole in the ground prepared for it. This shock disjointed the body, whose whole weight hung upon the nails, till the persons expired through mere dint of pain. This kind of death was used only by the Romans, and by them inflicted only on slaves and the vilest criminals.
The whole troop — or cohort. This was a body of foot commanded by the governor, which was appointed to prevent disorders and tumults, especially on solemn occasions. Mark xv, 16 John xix, 2.
They put on him a scarlet robe — Such as kings and generals wore; probably an old tattered one.
Him they compelled to bear his cross — He bore it himself, till he sunk under it, John xix, 17.

A place called Golgotha, that is, the place of a skull — Golgotha in Syriac signifies a skull or head: it was probably called so from this time; being an eminence upon Mount Calvary, not far from the king's gardens. Mark xv, 22; Luke xxiii, 33; John xix, 17

They gave him vinegar mingled with gall — Out of derision: which, however nauseous, he received and tasted of. St. Mark mentions also a different mixture which was given him, Wine mingled with myrrh: such as it was customary to give to dying criminals, to make them less sensible of their sufferings: but this our Lord refused to taste, determining to bear the full force of his pains.

They parted his garments — This was the custom of the Romams. The soldiers performed the office of executioners, and divided among them the spoils of the criminals. My vesture - That is, my inner garment. Psalm xxii, 18.
Mark xv, 27; Luke xxiii, 32.
Mark xv, 32; Luke xxiii, 33.

From the sixth hour, there was darkness over all the earth unto the ninth hour — Insomuch, that even a heathen philosopher seeing it, and knowing it could not be a natural eclipse, because it was at the time of the full moon, and continued three hours together, cried out, "Either the God of nature suffers, or the frame of the world is dissolved." By this darkness God testified his abhorrence of the wickedness which was then committing. It likewise intimated Christ's sore conflicts with the Divine justice, and with all the powers of darkness.

About the ninth hour, Jesus cried with a loud voice — Our Lord's great agony probably continued these three whole hours, at the conclusion of which be thus cried out, while he suffered from God himself what was unutterable. My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? - Our Lord hereby at once expresses his trust in God, and a most distressing sense of his letting loose the powers of darkness upon him, withdrawing the comfortable discoveries of his presence, and filling his soul with a terrible sense of the wrath due to the sins which he was bearing. Psalm xxii, 1.

One taking a sponge, filled it with vinegar — Vinegar and water was the usual drink of the Roman soldiers. It does not appear, that this was given him in derision, but rather with a friendly design, that he might not die before Elijah came. John xix, 28.

After he had cried with a loud voice — To show that his life was still whole in him. He dismissed his spirit - So the original expression may be literally translated: an expression admirably suited to our Lord's words, John x, xviii, No man taketh my life from me, but I lay it down of myself. He died by a voluntary act of his own, and in a way peculiar to himself. He alone of all men that ever were, could have continued alive even in the greatest tortures, as long as he pleased, or have retired from the body whenever he had thought fit. And how does it illustrate that love which he manifested in his death? Insomuch as he did not use his power to quit his body, as soon as it was fastened to the cross, leaving only an insensible corpse, to the cruelty of his murderers: but continued his abode in it, with a steady resolution, as long as it was proper. He then retired from it, with a majesty and dignity never known or to be known in any other death: dying, if one may so express it, like the Prince of life.

Immediately upon his death, while the sun was still darkened, the veil of the temple, which separated the holy of holies from the court of the priests, though made of the richest and strongest tapestry, was rent in two from the top to the bottom: so that while the priest was ministering at the golden altar (it being the time of the sacrifice) the sacred oracle, by an invisible power was laid open to full view: God thereby signifying the speedy removal of the veil of the Jewish ceremonies the casting down the partition wall, so that the Jews and Gentiles were now admitted to equal privileges, and the opening a way through the veil of his flesh for all believers into the most holy place. And the earth was shaken — There was a general earthquake through the whole globe, though chiefly near Jerusalem: God testifying thereby his wrath against the Jewish nation, for the horrid impiety they were committing.

Some of the tombs were shattered and laid open by the earthquake, and while they continued unclosed (and they must have stood open all the Sabbath, seeing the law would not allow any attempt to close them) many bodies of holy men were raised, (perhaps Simeon, Zacharias, John the Baptist, and others who had believed in Christ, and were known to many in Jerusalem, ) And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, went into the holy city (Jerusalem) and appeared to many — Who had probably known them before: God hereby signifying, that Christ had conquered death, and would raise all his saints in due season.

The centurion — The officer who commanded the guard; and they that were with him feared, saying, Truly this was the Son of God - Referring to the words of the chief priests and scribes, chap. xxvii, xliii, He said, I am the Son of God.
James — The less: he was so called, to distinguish him from the other James, the brother of John; probably because he was less in stature.
When the evening was come — That is, after three o'clock; the time from three to six they termed the evening. Mark xv, 42; Luke xxiii, 50; John xix, 38.

On the morrow, the day that followed the day of the preparation — The day of preparation was the day before the Sabbath, whereon they were to prepare for the celebration of it. The next day then was the Sabbath according to the Jews. But the evangelist seems to express it by this circumlocution, to show the Jewish Sabbath was then abolished.

That impostor said, while he was yet alive, After three days I will rise again — We do not find that he had ever said this to them, unless when he spoke of the temple of his body, John ii, 19, 21. And if they here refer to what he then said, how perverse and iniquitous was their construction on these words, when he was on his trial before the council? Chap. xxvi, 61. Then they seemed not to understand them!
Ye have a guard — Of your own, in the tower of Antonia, which was stationed there for the service of the temple.

They went and secured the sepulchre, sealing the stone, and setting a guard — They set Pilate's signet, or the public seal of the sanhedrim upon a fastening which they had put on the stone. And all this uncommon caution was overruled by the providence of God, to give the strongest proofs of Christ's ensuing resurrection; since there could be no room for the least suspicion of deceit, when it should be found, that his body was raised out of a new tomb, where there was no other corpse, and this tomb hewn out of a rock, the mouth of which was secured by a great stone, under a seal, and a guard of soldiers.

glossa.text: *What will you give.* Betraying him as though a worthless chattel, he puts it in the power of the buyers how much they will give.
*Where wilt thou,* etc. There was no fixed house for them: wherein the building of superfluous things is condemned.

*To a certain man.* He signifies the same man whom Mark and Luke call the master of the house. He therefore who says to a certain man, as though in his own person (and not the Lord's), for the sake of brevity indicated him in a summary way. *To a certain man.* Not to anyone whatever, but to some certain man, whom, speaking in his own person, he would rightly have set down. But now, when he has set down the words of the Lord, *Go ye into the city:* he himself puts in, *to a certain man:* not because the Lord said this, but that he himself might indicate to us, the proper name being left unspoken, that there was there a certain man to whom they were sent.

*And the disciples did even as.* In another Gospel it is written: *They found a large upper room furnished* . The upper room is the spiritual law, which, going forth from the straits of the letter, receives the Saviour in a lofty place. For he who follows the letter keeps the Pasch in the lowest place. But he who follows the water-bearer, that is, the herald of grace, into the house of the Church, he, transcending the letter by the spirit, prepares a refreshment for Christ in the height of the mind.

*That one of you.* He who foretold concerning the passion foretells concerning the betrayer, that seeing himself not to be hidden he might repent of the deed. He casts the charge upon the number, that the guilty one might do penance, yet he does not point him out particularly, lest he should become more shameless.
*They began every one.* Because they believe the master more than themselves: and fearing also their own frailty, they ask concerning a sin of which they have no knowledge in themselves.

*He that dippeth.* While the others were made sorrowful and were drawing back their hand from the food, with that shamelessness with which he betrayed him he puts his hand in with the master, that by boldness he might feign a good conscience. Behold the humility and the patience with which he admits the betrayer to the table. *In the dish.* Mark: *in the bowl.* A paropsis is a four-cornered vessel for food, so called from equal apsides, that is, from equal sides: a catinum is an earthen vessel fit for pouring in liquid, and it could happen that the table held a vessel both earthen and four-cornered. The penalty is foretold, that the punishments declared might correct him whom shame had not overcome.

*It were better for him.* It would be much better not to be at all than to be in evil case, he says this in the customary and simple way. For it cannot be well with him who is not. Or does he say to the devil, not to be born unto sin: or was it also good for him that he should not be born to Christ by calling, lest he should be an apostate by betrayal? Or we are wont to say simply, it would be better not to be than to be in evil case.

*Rabbi.* The others say, Lord, this man, Rabbi. As though it were a lesser sin to betray a master than the Lord, or else by way of flattery.
*Thou hast said it.* Nor is it openly said here whether it was he: for it can be understood as though he were saying, I did not say it.

*And whilst they were at supper,* etc. The solemn joys of the old Pasch being ended, which were kept in memory of the deliverance of the people of God out of Egypt, he passes over to the new, which he willed the Church to frequent in memory of himself. Namely, that in place of the flesh and blood of the lamb he might substitute the sacrament of his own body and blood, and might show that he is the one to whom *the Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent: thou art a priest ((Psal. CIX))*, etc. *He took. ((HIER.))* After the typical Pasch had been fulfilled, and he had eaten the flesh of the lamb with the apostles, he takes bread. *And blessed and broke.* Because he so subjected the man he had assumed to death, that he showed the power of immortality to be in him, and that therefore he would rise again quickly. *He broke,* that he might show that the breaking of his body would not be without his own will. He blessed first, because the nature which he assumed he filled, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, with the grace of divine power. Therefore he gave his body after supper, because it was necessary that the typical Pasch should first be completed, and that so the sacraments should afterwards be substituted for the old Pasch. But we, for reverence of so great a sacrament, are refreshed with the sacraments of the Lord's passion before bodily food.

*He gave thanks.* He shows what each one ought to do under the scourge of his own fault, since he himself bore with an even mind the scourge of another's: because bread strengthens the body, wine produces blood.

*I will not drink.* I will not take delight in the ceremonies of this people, among which the rites of the paschal lamb are chief. After the passion I will not take up flesh, until I take it up new, which is now mortal.

*New in the kingdom of the Father.* Calling that *new,* and this old, he shows the body: namely, that which is of the old Adam, which shall be changed by immortality. *With you,* by this immortality is promised to his own also, although not at the same time. *Of this fruit,* because the same bodies are to rise again. But the day of my resurrection will be when, exalted in the kingdom of God, that is, in the glory of immortality, I shall be filled with a new joy together with you over the salvation of that same people regenerated by spiritual grace.

*And a hymn.* This is what the psalm says: *The poor shall eat and shall be filled ((Psal. XXI))*, etc. Or, according to John, he sang a hymn giving thanks to the Father, in which he prayed for himself and for the disciples and for those who should believe. *They went out unto the mount,* etc. That through the receiving of the sacraments and through his own intercession he may teach us to ascend to higher gifts, with which we are anointed in heart: where is the refreshment of labour, the solace of sorrow.
*That you all suffer scandal* . He foretells to them what they are to suffer, that afterwards they may not then despair, but be set free by penance.

*After.* As he foretold the place of the passion, so he foretells the place of the resurrection, that as they are sorrowful from the passion, so they may rejoice, glorified by the resurrection or by the vision. *I will go before you,* etc. That he might console their weakness by the promise of his own return.
*And if all.* It is not a lie nor rashness, but faith and burning love, to such a degree that he did not look to his own weakness nor to the trustworthiness of the words of God.
*And pray.* Death being close at hand, he fitly prays in the valley of fatness, because through humility and the fatness of charity he underwent death for us.

*He began to grow sorrowful.* Not from fear of the passion, since he had come for this, but on account of the scandal of the apostles and the perdition of the ungodly. *((HIER.)) He began to grow sorrowful,* that he might prove the truth of the man he had assumed. He was truly made sorrowful, but the passion does not rule over his mind: rather it is a propassion, whence he says: *He began to grow sorrowful.* But he is made sorrowful not from fear of suffering, since he had come for this, but on account of the unhappy Judas and the scandal of the apostles and the casting out of the Jews and the overthrow of Jerusalem.

*Sorrowful.* It is the soul that fears and is made sorrowful. Peter, the lesser, does not fear, saying: *I will lay down my life for thee:* because, as a man, he does not know the force of death. Christ fears, because, as God set within a body, he sets forth the frailty of the flesh: he who took a body was bound to undergo all things that belong to a body.

*Even unto death. ((HIL.))* Not because of death, but until he should free the apostles by his own passion. It is not death, but the time of death, that is in fear, because after the power of the resurrection the faith of believers is to be strengthened.

*If it be possible.* This not out of fear, but out of mercy, lest the Jews, who have not the excuse of ignorance, should not kill him *non occidant*; read *occidant*, "should kill him"; whence he says: *this,* that is, the cup of the people of the Jews, not simply a cup: *If it be possible* that the Gentiles may believe without the destruction of the Jews, I refuse the passion. But if they are to be blinded that the Gentiles may come in, let not my will, but thine be done. *Not as I will. ((AUG.))* He transfigures his own into himself, who wills nothing other than the Father, as in that place: *I was hungry, and you gave me to eat. And why persecutest thou me?* But he teaches them to correct their own private will and to direct it according to the divine. ((AMBR.)) The man whom he showed forth by the truth of a body, he made equal in affection, so as to say: *But not as I will, but as thou* . He took up my will, he took up my sorrow. Confidently do I name sorrow, I who preach the cross.
*But the flesh.* He says this assuredly not of himself, but of those who said that they would never deny him.

*Again a second time.* He prays a second time, that is, if Nineveh cannot be saved otherwise, unless the gourd wither, that is, the people of the Jews, who before were his tabernacle, so that it may kill me.

*He prayed the third time.* He prayed three times over, that we too may pray for pardon from past sins, and for protection from the evils we repent of, and for wariness against future perils, and that we may direct every prayer to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Likewise, as there is a threefold temptation of desire, so also of fear. For there is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes and the ambition of the world. There is also the fear of death, and the fear of advantage, and the fear of pain, against all which he teaches that we ought to be fortified by prayer. Whence also, on account of the threefold temptation of the passion, it can be understood that the Lord prayed three times.
*With swords and clubs.* The deed agrees with the changed mind. For now he comes with clubs who, so long as he was at peace, bore himself more quietly.

*He gave them a sign* . He thought that the signs which he had seen were done not by divine power, but by magic: and him whom he had heard was transfigured upon the mountain he feared lest in some such way he should now slip out of their hands: and therefore he gave a sign. *Whomsoever I shall kiss.* He still had something of the modesty of a disciple, in that he did not betray him openly to persecutions, but by the sign of a kiss.

*And he kissed him.* The Lord received the kiss, not that he might teach us to dissemble, but lest he should seem to flee the betrayal, whence: *With them that hated peace I was peaceable ((Psal. CXIX))*.
*They shall perish with the sword.* With that sword which, being of fire, is turned before paradise, that is, of divine vengeance, and with the sword of the spirit, that is, of the word of God.

*Thinkest thou that,* etc. As if he should say, I have no need of the help of the twelve apostles, I who can have twelve legions of angels, in which are seventy-two thousand, by which the tongue of all nations is expressed. But he intimates that it is not to be feared if all nations rise up against Jesus, since he himself has far stronger armies of angels. Otherwise: This number signifies the whole race of men that was to contend with the Roman empire against the Jews. These are the angels of God, who in the forty-second year after the resurrection, together with Titus and Vespasian, destroyed those murderers and burned their city.

*You are come out with swords.* It is foolish to seek with swords and clubs him who gives himself up of his own accord, and to track down by night through a betrayer, as though he were in hiding, one who taught daily in the temple. But you gather together in the darkness, because your power is in the darkness.

*To Caiphas.* The name agrees with the deed. Caiphas, that is, a searcher out, or shrewd to fulfil, namely, the wickedness of his own guile. Or, one vomiting with the mouth, because he was shameless in uttering a lie and in demanding a murder.

*Afar off.* Rightly afar off, he who was about to deny him close at hand, he signifies the Church, which would imitate the passion of Christ far differently, because the Church suffers for itself, but Christ for the Church.

*Thou hast said it.* Mark: *I am:* which is the same: And there is a like answer against Pilate and against Caiphas, that they may be condemned out of their own sentence. *The Son of man.* Me, exalted in the form which you judge, and having the name which is above every name.

*He rent his garments.* The fury which made him rise from his seat makes him also rend his garment. By a great mystery: since the garment of the Lord could not be rent even by the soldiers. For it signifies that their priesthood, the pontificate, was for their crimes to be utterly dissolved: but the solidity of the Church (which is called the garment of God) will remain unbroken to the end of the world. It is the custom of the Jews, when they hear anything of blasphemy, they rend their garments.

Which Paul and Barnabas did in Lycaonia, when they were called Jupiter and Apollo.

*Then they spit.* As he was then spit upon with the spittle of unbelievers, so now he is dishonoured with the reproaches of false believers, and is beaten with buffets, that is, with the blasphemies of the same men.

*Prophesy.* They speak an insult to him who willed to be held a prophet by the peoples. For they veiled his face, according to Mark, not that he might not see their crimes, but that they might hide from themselves the grace of the knowledge of him. As there was a veil upon the face of Moses, which remains to this day.

*One maidservant.* Why does a maidservant betray him first, when the men were better able to recognize him, unless that this sex might be shown to have sinned unto the death of the Lord: and redeemed through the passion. And therefore a woman first received the mystery of the resurrection: and kept the commands, that she might abolish the old error of the transgression. As through a woman the ancient enemy seduced the first parent, so through a woman he drives the prince of the Church to deny the master whom he had confessed to be Christ the Son of God.
*I know not the man.* How harmful are the conversations of the wicked, which compel Peter to deny Christ, or that he knew the man whom he confessed among the disciples to be the Son of God.

*They that stood by.* John and Luke speak of one, a kinsman of Malchus. But either it is a plural for a singular. Or there was one who had seen him and was speaking chiefly, whom the rest, following him, accused in like manner.

*And immediately the cock crew.* After the third denial the cock's crowing follows. The sacraments of things are signified by the state of the times. At midnight he denies, at the cock's crowing he repents, after the resurrection, in the light, he professed three times that he loved him whom he had three times denied: because what he had erred in the darkness of forgetfulness, he corrected by the remembrance of the light already hoped for: and by the presence of that same true light he fully raised up whatever he had changed.

*He remembered.* In another Gospel it is said, *The Lord looked upon Peter ((Luc. XXII))*, and by his look drew him to tears, as though bringing back to his mind how often he had denied, and what he had foretold to him, nor could he remain in darkness upon whom the light of the world had looked. *And going forth.* Shut off from the counsel of the ungodly, he washes away his fault, which he did not do within. For this cause he was permitted to waver, that in the prince of the Church a remedy of penance might be established, and that no one should dare to trust in his own strength.

*And in the morning.* Matthew and Mark have woven together the narrative of the things that were done with the Lord up to the morning, but afterwards they go back to tell the denial of Peter: which being ended, they return again to the morning, that from there they might weave together the rest.

VERS. 4. *I have sinned in betraying,* etc. As though it were in his own power to change the sentence of the persecutors: but although he changed his will, yet he did not change the outcome of his first will. *What is that to us.* What does it concern us about this? *look thou to it,* do thou know what thou hast done. Or, what dost thou see as pertaining to us. What does the price received concern us: thou hadst approved of that, do thou with it what thou wilt. They who sin unto death have so great ignorance and blindness that they are neither troubled in their crimes, nor tormented with the pain of repentance.

*And casting down.* As his repentance was fruitless, so also this offering in the temple is execrable. *And going away. ((HIER.))* It profited Judas nothing to have done penance, by which he could not correct his crime. But when a brother so sins against a brother that he is able to amend what he has sinned, it can be forgiven him. But if the works remain, penance is taken up with the voice in vain. This is what is said of him: *And let his prayer be turned to sin ((Psal. CVIII))*: so that not only was he unable to amend the wickedness of the betrayal, but he added the crime of his own murder, whence he was the more wicked.

*It is not lawful for them.* Truly straining out the gnat and swallowing the camel: for if for this reason they do not put the money into the corbona, that is, into the treasury, that is, among the gifts of God, because it is the price of blood, why then is the blood itself poured out? And what reward is theirs, if from it a field is bought for the burial of the poor?

*By Jeremias. ((HIER.))* This is read not in Jeremias, but in Zacharias: yet in other words. I lately read an apocryphon of Jeremias, in which I found these words written. But nevertheless it seems to me rather that this was taken from Zacharias, after the manner of the apostles, who, the order of the words being passed over, bring forward only the meanings out of the Old Testament.

*Of the children of Israel,* etc. From whom it was less fitting, who ought to have magnified him.

*Thou art the king of the Jews.* According to Luke they had brought two charges, namely that he forbade tribute to be given to Caesar, and that he said he was a king. Concerning the kingdom, therefore, Pilate asks, because he does not know it. Concerning the tributes: because he had heard that he had answered: *Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's ((Zac. II))*: he disregards, as it were, the open lie of the envious. Whence Mark: *And their testimonies were not agreeing ((Marc. XXIV))* . In this, that Pilate asks of no other crime except whether he is the king of the Jews: the Jews are convicted of impiety, who could not even falsely find what they might lay against the Saviour.

*Who was called Barabbas.* Barabbas, in the Gospel according to the Hebrews, is interpreted *son of the father* or *their master.* He himself is Antichrist, whom they prefer to Christ, to whom it is said: *You are of your father the devil ((Joan. VIII))*. Pilate, who is interpreted *the mouth of the hammerer,* signifies the devil, who is the hammer of the whole earth, by whom the Lord permits his own vessels to be tried: and at the last he grinds him down, when in the final damnation he shall break him in pieces.

*Whom will you.* Wishing to satisfy the people, he gives the choice, although he does not doubt that Christ is to be chosen, knowing that he had been handed over through envy. *Who is called Christ.* The same as what Mark says: the king of the Jews, whose king Christ was called.

*For the judgment seat.* The tribunal is the seat of judges, as the throne is of kings, the chair of teachers. *His wife.* The wife of a Gentile man understands in a vision that which the Jews, waking, would not understand. *Have thou nothing to do with that just man.* Now at last the devil, understanding that through Christ he was to lose his spoils, just as at the first he brought in death through a woman; so now through a woman he wishes to free Christ out of the hands of the Jews, lest through his death he lose the empire of death.

*Barabbas,* etc. They chose the son of the devil instead of the Son of God, that they might destroy the Saviour together with their own salvation, and set free a betrayer, which petition of theirs cleaves to them even to this day, their nation and their place and their liberty being lost: because they willed to destroy the giver of liberty.

*What therefore shall I do with Jesus.* He sought many occasions to set him free with the goodwill of the people. First, comparing a robber with a just man. Then: *What then shall I do with Jesus, who is called Christ?* And when they said: *let him be crucified,* he did not at once yield, but according to his wife's suggestion he says: *Why, what evil hath he done?* By which saying Pilate absolved Christ.
*He washed his hands.* Signifying the Gentile people, a stranger to the impiety of the Jews, who cried out: *Crucify him, crucify him.*
*His blood.* The imprecation persists to this day, and the blood of Christ is not taken away from them.

*Then he released to them Barabbas.* Barabbas, a seditious robber and the author of murders, was released to the people of the Jews. ((ISID.)) The devil, who long since had for his pride been driven out of the fatherland of light, and had been sent into the prison of darkness. And therefore the Jews cannot have peace, because they chose rather the prince of seditions. Or, Barabbas bore the type of Antichrist.

*But Jesus having been scourged* . Therefore it is to be believed that Pilate scourged Jesus and gave him to the soldiers to be mocked, that the Jews, sated with his punishments and his reproaches, might thirst no further for his death. *But Jesus.* Serving the Roman laws, which command that those who are to be crucified be first scourged.

*A scarlet cloak. ((HIER.))* In the scarlet cloak he bears up the bloody works of the Gentiles. In the crown of thorns he looses the ancient curse. In the reed he kills the venomous beasts. Or he holds the reed in his hand, that he might write the sacrilege of the Jews. He is not mocked in his own garments, but in those which he bore for our sins. When he was crucified he received his own adornment at once: because the elements are troubled, and the creature gives testimony to the Creator.
*A man of Cyrene.* Behold, not a Hebrew, but a foreigner is put under the reproach of Christ, that the fulness of the sacraments might be shown to pass over from circumcision to uncircumcision.

*Golgotha.* It is Syriac, and is interpreted *of Calvary,* not because of the baldness of Adam, whom they falsely say was buried there, but because of the beheading of the condemned. Adam is read in the book of Josue to have been buried near Hebron.

*Mingled with gall.* Another evangelist says *myrrhed,* that is, most bitter. And there could have been a mingling of both, of gall and of myrrh. *And when he had tasted, he would not.* This Mark passes over in silence: *he would not drink.* This is what Mark says: *he took it not,* namely, that he should drink it.

*They divided.* This John more distinctly: the garments into four parts, that the Church may be signified in the four parts of the world. The coat allotted signifies the unity of all the parts by the bond of charity, which comes about by lot, that is, by the grace of God, not by human choice.
*The cause.* For which the Jews handed him over to Pilate. The King through the cross did not lose, but confirmed, his empire, whether the Jews will or will not.

*One on the right hand.* One on the right hand, by whom is signified the mortification of the flesh for the sake of heavenly glory: one on the left hand, by whom again is signified the mortification of the flesh for the sake of some cause of the world.

*They blasphemed.* It had been foretold in the book of Wisdom ((Cap. II)): *Let us condemn him to a most shameful death. For there shall be respect in his words. For if he be truly the Son of God, he will take him up and will deliver him from the hand of his adversaries* . Because therefore he was being crucified and was not delivered, they believed that he was not the Son of God: therefore they insult him as he hangs upon the tree, and shake their heads:
*If thou be the Son of God.* If, yielding to those who insulted him, he had come down from the cross, he would not have shown the power of patience.

*And we will believe him* . A fraudulent promise: he does a greater thing in rising from the tomb, and you do not believe: if therefore he should come down from the cross, you would not believe. But the demons put this in; for they felt at once the power of the cross, and their own strength broken, and they do this that he may come down from the cross. But the Lord, knowing this, remains, that he may destroy the devil.

*And the selfsame thing the robbers also.* At first both blasphemed, then, the signs being seen, one believed. So both peoples first blasphemed God: but the one, terrified by the signs, repented, and now convicts the Jews.

*And from the sixth hour.* Note that the Lord is crucified when the sun is about to withdraw from the centre of the world, because he dies for sins, and Adam, when he had sinned, heard the voice of the Lord after midday. And it is the order of reason that at the time at which he shut the gate of paradise against the transgressing Adam, at that time he should unlock it to the penitent robber. That Mark says the Lord was crucified at the third hour is for this reason, that he may show that the Jews, who excuse themselves, crucified him rather with their tongues than the soldiers by whose hands it was done: who at the third hour cried out that he should be crucified. For when he was crucified, it was about the sixth hour, that is, not yet fully the sixth.

*And about the ninth hour.* When the day had declined toward evening and the sun had grown cool from its heat, he completes the passion, showing that he dies for our sins, by which we have fallen from the divine light and love into this night. In the morning the Lord rose again, teaching that he would lead forth those raised up in soul into the light of eternal happiness. *Eli, Eli, lamma.* Whose nature he takes upon him, of the same men he bewails the misery. Wherein he shows how much they themselves ought to weep who sin. Marvel not at the lowliness of the words and at the complaints of one forsaken, since, knowing the form of a servant, thou seest the scandal of the cross.
*And certain.* Not all, perhaps Romans, not knowing the property of the Hebrew speech. Or some Jews, reckoning Christ less than Elias, so that he should beg his help.
*Let be, let us see.* Because they understood the voice of the Lord amiss, they waited in vain for the coming of Elias.

*And behold the veil of the temple.* That the ark of the testament and all the sacraments of the law, which were being covered, might appear and might pass over to the Gentiles. Josephus says that the angelic powers, once the guardians of the temple, then cried out together: let us pass over from these seats. The veil which was called the outer one: because now we see in part; but when that which is perfect shall come, then the inner veil shall be rent asunder. *The earth was moved.* All the elements show forth their Lord crucified. The earth is moved, not enduring to bear its Lord as he hangs. *The rocks.* That is, the hearts of the Gentiles, or the prophecies of the prophets, who are called rocks from the rock Christ, that whatever in them was shut up under the hard veil of the law might, being rent, lie open to the Gentiles.

*And the monuments.* And yet, although the monuments were opened, they did not rise before the Lord rose again, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. *The bodies of the saints.* These are to be believed to have ascended in like manner with the body when the Lord ascended.
*Into the holy city.* Jerusalem, which is called holy because of the temple, and the Holy of holies, which no other city has.

*And the centurion.* These men confess God in the scandal of the cross. Arius in the Church preaches a creature, whom the blind Jews do not believe even for so many miracles. In the centurion is signified the faith of the Church, which, the veil of the heavenly mysteries being unlocked by the death of the Lord, affirms Jesus to be the Son of God while the Synagogue is silent.

*Many women.* Matthew and Luke say that Mary Magdalen stood afar off. But John says she was beside the cross, because she was distant by such an interval that she could be said to be beside it: because she was at hand in his sight, and afar off by comparison with the nearer crowd. We can also say that those women who were with the mother of the Lord, after he had commended her to the disciple, had already begun to go away, that they might draw themselves out of the density of the crowd and behold from farther off the other things that were done. *Ministering unto him.* It was of the Hebrew custom that women should minister of their own substance to their teachers: which the Lord accepted, that he might give an example to the apostles.
*Of James.* James the son of Alphaeus is called the less, to distinguish him from that James who was called among the first apostles and chosen by the Lord.

*A rich man.* Because none but a rich man could approach the governor, not that the evangelist commends riches. He was called also a decurion, because he was of the order of the curia and discharged the office of the curia, by this he could have the means, by this, that he was a disciple, he was worthy of this ministry. *He was a disciple of Jesus. He went to Pilate.* Although in secret, avoiding beforehand the enmities of the Jews, in this last office he cares nothing for them.

*In a clean linen cloth.* Mystically. He wraps Jesus in a clean linen cloth who receives him with a pure mind. Hence also the custom of the Church holds that the sacrifice of the altar be celebrated not upon silk, not upon dyed cloth, but upon pure linen.

*In his own new monument.* Because, if he were laid in a monument where another had been laid, another perhaps would be feigned to have risen again. In the rock, lest, if it had been built of many stones, he should be said to have been taken away by theft, the foundations of the tomb being undermined.

*And there were there.* While the other acquaintances of Jesus were returning to their own, the women alone, who loved more closely, were watching the service of the burial, awaiting what Jesus had promised: and therefore they are the first to see the resurrection.

*After three.* The whole from a part, of the sixth day, on which he was crucified, with its own night, for one day. The sabbath entire. The third day from its first part, that is, from the night, for the whole with its own daytime, and so there is a space of three days.
*They made the sepulchre sure.* Their diligence profited our faith. For the more it was guarded, the more is the power of the resurrection shown.

registers.label: Spare
lines: He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.
He humbled himself and obeyed, even to death.
He did not hide his face from shame and spitting.
Into your hands, O Lord, we commit our spirits.
At the table he gave the bread and the cup.
This is my body; this is my blood, poured out for you.
Come, let us worship the One who goes to the cross.
Do not be far from us, O Lord. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: The shouting of Sunday has died down; now the table is set in an upper room, and the bread is broken, and the cup is poured out.
Do not be far from us, O Lord.
The servant gives his back to those who strike, his cheeks to those who pull the beard, and does not turn his face away.
Do not be far from us, O Lord.
Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, took the form of a slave, and became obedient even to death on a cross.
Do not be far from us, O Lord.
Into the long night he goes, betrayed with a kiss, abandoned in a garden, handed over to the powers.
Do not be far from us, O Lord.
So every knee shall bend and every tongue confess that he is Lord. Come, let us worship and follow him down.
Do not be far from us, O Lord; into your hands we commit our spirits. Amen.
